At its core, this technique relies on a two-stage process: a fast "draft" model proposes a sequence of future tokens, and a slower, high-quality "target" model verifies these proposals in a single forward pass. The efficiency of this system hinges entirely on the verification mechanism, which must ensure that the final output is statistically identical to what the target model would have produced on its own, while simultaneously maximizing the number of accepted tokens per verification step.

When the target model processes the draft sequence, it computes the probability distribution for the next token at each position in the draft. If the target model’s probability is higher than or equal to the draft model’s, the token is accepted immediately. However, if the target model assigns a lower probability to the drafted token than the draft model did, the token is not automatically rejected. Instead, it is accepted with a probability proportional to the ratio of the target’s probability to the draft’s probability. This probabilistic acceptance ensures that the final distribution of tokens matches the target model’s distribution exactly, preserving the quality and diversity of the output.
